A decision tree classifies an example with a sequence of simple tests, such as “is the age below 25?”, and the answers lead to a label. Trees are easy to read for humans and fast to evaluate for machines, they handle discrete and continuous features without normalization, and they can be written down as rules. A single tree is rarely the best classifier, but ensembles of trees are among the most accurate methods for tabular data today. This section shows how a tree is learned from data with the ID3 and C4.5 algorithms, how pruning keeps it from overfitting, and how random forests and gradient boosting combine many trees.
Classification trees are older than computers.

shows a classification scheme from the botanical writings of Carl Linnaeus, who organized plants and animals in such hierarchies from 1735 on. Each bracket is a test on one characteristic, each branch a possible outcome, and the leaves are the classes. The tree is not balanced: some leaves are reached after two tests, others after five.

Ross Quinlan’s ID3 algorithm (1986) builds a tree from the top down. It chooses the feature whose test best separates the classes, splits the training examples by the values of that feature, and repeats the procedure for each subset until a subset contains a single class or no features are left. Each feature is used at most once on a path, so the depth of the tree is limited by the number of features.

children.value: Quinlan’s C4.5 algorithm (1993) extends ID3 in several ways and became one of the most widely used classifiers; a survey of data mining algorithms in 2008 ranked it first. Two extensions matter most.

are split with a threshold. C4.5 sorts the training examples by the feature value and considers a threshold between each pair of neighbors with different labels, typically at the midpoint. Each candidate is scored with the information gain of the resulting binary split. Unlike a discrete feature, a continuous feature may be tested again further down the tree, with a different threshold.

Six days have the temperatures 40, 48, 60, 72, 80, 90 and the labels No, No, Yes, Yes, Yes, No, with an entropy of 1 bit. A tree that grows until every leaf is pure fits the training data perfectly, including its noise and its exceptions, and generalizes poorly. Two kinds of
stops the growth early: a node becomes a leaf if it holds too few examples or if the best split gains too little.
grows the full tree first and then simplifies it with a validation set, as described in

. It visits the inner nodes, tentatively replaces the subtree below a node by a leaf with the most common label, and keeps the replacement if the accuracy on the validation set does not drop. It repeats this until no replacement helps.

C4.5 can also prune the rules instead of the tree. It removes conditions from each rule as long as the accuracy improves. The rules are then no longer mutually exclusive, so C4.5 sorts them by their accuracy and applies the first rule that matches.

Real training data also needs preparation before a tree is grown. Examples without a label are removed, outliers eliminated, and missing feature values predicted or treated as a value of their own. Identical feature vectors with conflicting labels are collapsed into one entry with the most frequent label, keeping their count so that the entropies remain correct. Features that cannot help, such as a date or an identifier, are removed. Most of this work is specific to the domain: a good tree depends more on a small set of informative, weakly correlated features than on the learning algorithm.
A single tree is unstable. A small change in the training data can change the feature chosen at the root and thereby the whole tree, so trees have a high variance in the sense of
. Ensembles average many trees to reduce this variance.

(Breiman 2001) trains hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training set, drawn with replacement, and each split considers only a random subset of the features. The randomness makes the trees differ, and their majority vote is far more accurate and stable than any single tree.

The learning rate keeps each tree from correcting too much at once, and the number of trees and their depth are hyperparameters chosen on validation data. With other losses, the trees fit other gradients: the logistic loss for classification, or the pairwise ranking gradients of LambdaMART for the learning-to-rank models of
. Libraries such as XGBoost and LightGBM implement gradient boosting efficiently, and on tabular data with mixed feature types, gradient-boosted trees often outperform neural networks.
